summary: Describes the Internet Key Exchange, a hybrid protocol that negotiates security associations and produces authenticated keying material for IPsec. It combines pieces of ISAKMP and OAKLEY. This first version is now historic, replaced by RFC 4306.

plainLanguage.summary: Before two computers can talk privately, they must agree on a shared secret without anyone overhearing. IKE is the careful conversation they have to do that. It runs in two rounds: first a protected channel is set up, then fresh keys for the traffic itself are agreed.

subtitle: The original key exchange for IPsec: two phases that set up a protected channel and then negotiate fresh keys.

tldr.problem: ISAKMP provides a framework for authentication and key exchange but does not define the exchanges themselves, so IPsec needed a concrete way to negotiate security associations and authenticated keying material.
tldr.mechanism: IKE combines part of Oakley and part of SKEME with ISAKMP. In phase 1, Main Mode or Aggressive Mode builds an authenticated ISAKMP security association using Diffie-Hellman; in phase 2, Quick Mode negotiates the security associations for services such as AH and ESP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2409 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 4306 and updated by RFC 4109.

sections.title: Introduction: A Hybrid Key Exchange
sections.content:
ISAKMP provides a framework for authentication and key exchange but does not define them; it is designed to be key exchange independent, so that it can support many different key exchanges. Oakley describes a series of key exchanges, called modes, and the services each one provides, such as perfect forward secrecy, identity protection and authentication. SKEME describes a key exchange technique that provides anonymity, repudiability and quick key refreshment.

RFC 2409 describes a protocol that uses part of Oakley and part of SKEME together with ISAKMP to obtain authenticated keying material, both for ISAKMP itself and for other security associations such as AH and ESP in the IETF IPsec Domain of Interpretation. The memo calls this a hybrid protocol, and its purpose is to negotiate security associations and supply authenticated keying material for them in a protected manner.

Processes that implement the memo can be used for negotiating virtual private networks, and for giving a remote user access from a remote site whose IP address need not be known beforehand to a secure host or network. Client negotiation is supported, meaning the two negotiating parties need not be the endpoints of the security association; in that case the identities of the end parties remain hidden. The memo implements only a subset of Oakley and only the public key encryption method and the fast re-keying idea of SKEME, and it does not depend on either protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IKE is the conversation two machines have before they send protected traffic. They agree on an encryption algorithm, a way to check messages, a way to prove who they are, and a shared secret that only they know.

sections.title: Phases, Modes and Security Associations
sections.content:
A security association is a set of policy and keys used to protect information. The ISAKMP security association is the shared policy and keys that the negotiating peers use to protect their own communication. Oakley defines modes and ISAKMP defines phases, and IKE presents its exchanges as modes that operate in one of two phases.

Phase 1 is where the two peers establish a secure, authenticated channel to communicate over, which is the ISAKMP security association. Main Mode and Aggressive Mode each accomplish a phase 1 exchange, and neither may be used anywhere else. Phase 2 is where security associations are negotiated on behalf of services such as IPsec, and Quick Mode accomplishes a phase 2 exchange. New Group Mode is neither phase 1 nor phase 2: it follows phase 1 and establishes a new Diffie-Hellman group for use in future negotiations.

The ISAKMP security association is bidirectional, so once it exists either party may start a Quick Mode, Informational or New Group Mode exchange. It is identified by the initiator's cookie followed by the responder's cookie, and the cookie order set during phase 1 keeps identifying it no matter which direction a later exchange runs, so the cookies must not swap places when the direction changes.

Phase 1 negotiates four attributes, and all of them are mandatory: the encryption algorithm, the hash algorithm, the authentication method and information about a Diffie-Hellman group. A pseudo-random function may also be negotiated; if it is not, the HMAC version of the negotiated hash algorithm is used instead. Implementations must support DES in CBC mode with a weak and semi-weak key check, MD5 and SHA, authentication with pre-shared keys, and Diffie-Hellman over default group one, and should support 3DES, Tiger, DSA and RSA signatures, RSA public key encryption and group two.
sections.plainLanguage: The work is split in two. The first phase sets up a protected channel between the two machines. The second phase uses that channel to agree the keys for the traffic that follows. A single first phase can serve many later phases, which saves round trips.

sections.title: Phase 1 Exchanges and Authentication Methods
sections.content:
There are two basic methods for establishing an authenticated key exchange, Main Mode and Aggressive Mode, and each generates authenticated keying material from an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange. Main Mode must be implemented and Aggressive Mode should be. Exchanges are not open ended: they have a fixed number of messages, and a Certificate Request payload must not extend that number.

Main Mode is the ISAKMP Identity Protect exchange. The first two messages negotiate policy, the next two exchange Diffie-Hellman public values and a nonce, and the last two authenticate the exchange. Aggressive Mode is the ISAKMP Aggressive exchange: the first two messages negotiate policy, exchange the public values, a nonce and the identities, and the second message also authenticates the responder, while the third authenticates the initiator. Aggressive Mode saves a round trip but limits what can be negotiated, because the Diffie-Hellman group cannot be negotiated and some authentication methods restrict the cipher and hash as well.

Four authentication methods are allowed in either mode: digital signatures, two forms of authentication with public key encryption, and a pre-shared key. With signatures, the ancillary information exchanged in the second round trip is a nonce, and the exchange is authenticated by signing a hash that both sides can compute. With public key encryption, the ancillary information is an encrypted nonce, and each party's ability to reconstruct the hash proves that the other party decrypted the nonce; the identities are encrypted with the other party's public key as well, and only the bodies of the payloads are encrypted. The revised form of public key encryption keeps the advantages but halves the public key operations, because the peer's identity is encrypted with the negotiated symmetric algorithm instead of the public key. The nonces are exchanged in the clear.

The length of a nonce payload must be between 8 and 256 bytes inclusive. The result of either mode is three groups of authenticated keying material: SKEYID_d, used to derive keys for security associations other than ISAKMP; SKEYID_a, used to authenticate the messages of the ISAKMP security association; and SKEYID_e, used to protect their confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Main Mode takes six messages and hides the identities of the two peers. Aggressive Mode takes three and gives that protection up, but asks less of the machines. Either way the peers exchange Diffie-Hellman values, send a nonce, and then prove who they are.

sections.title: Quick Mode and Fresh Keys
sections.content:
Quick Mode is essentially a security association negotiation and an exchange of nonces, and the nonces give replay protection. They are used to generate fresh key material and to stop a replayed packet from producing bogus security associations. An optional Key Exchange payload can be carried, which allows an additional Diffie-Hellman exchange and exponentiation for that exchange; the payload is optional but must be supported.

Base Quick Mode, without the Key Exchange payload, refreshes the key material derived from the phase 1 exponentiation and therefore does not give perfect forward secrecy. With the optional payload, an extra exponentiation is performed and perfect forward secrecy is provided for the key material. A single negotiation produces two security associations, one inbound and one outbound, with a different security parameters index for each so that the two directions use different keys.

Several security associations can be negotiated in one Quick Mode exchange, and the resulting key material is derived the same way. Where more key material is needed than the pseudo-random function produces, the output is fed back into itself and the results are concatenated until the amount required is reached. The memo notes that the exponential from a Quick Mode exchange is irrecoverably removed from the current state, while SKEYID_e and SKEYID_a continue to protect the ISAKMP security association.

The identities of the security associations negotiated in Quick Mode are implicitly the IP addresses of the ISAKMP peers, unless client identifiers are given. When ISAKMP acts as a client negotiator on behalf of another party, the identities of the parties must be passed as IDci and then IDcr, so that traffic can be directed to the right tunnel when several tunnels exist between two peers. If the client identities are not acceptable to the responder, a Notify payload with message type INVALID-ID-INFORMATION should be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Quick Mode is how the two peers renew the keys for the traffic they are protecting. It normally reuses the secret from the first phase, and the optional key exchange payload buys a fresh secret at the cost of one more calculation on each side.

sections.title: Oakley Groups and New Group Mode
sections.content:
The group in which the Diffie-Hellman exchange is performed is negotiated. Four groups, with values 1 through 4, are defined in the memo; they came from the Oakley protocol and are therefore called Oakley Groups, and all values of 2^15 and higher are used for private group identifiers. All four were generated by Richard Schroeppel at the University of Arizona.

Group 1 is a MODP group with a prime given as 2^768 - 2^704 - 1 + 2^64 * { [2^638 pi] + 149686 } and generator 2, and implementations must support it. Group 2 is a MODP group with the prime 2^1024 - 2^960 - 1 + 2^64 * { [2^894 pi] + 129093 } and generator 2, which implementations should support. Groups 3 and 4 are EC2N groups: group 3 is based on the Galois field GF[2^155] with field size 155 and irreducible polynomial u^155 + u^62 + 1, and group 4 is based on GF[2^185] with field size 185 and irreducible polynomial u^185 + u^69 + 1. In both elliptic curve groups the data in the Key Exchange payload is the x value of a point on the curve, and either of the two possible y values may be used, since the parties need not agree on the choice.

New Group Mode must not be used before an ISAKMP security association exists, and it describes a new group that can be used in later negotiations. The proposal gives the characteristics of the group, and private group descriptions must be greater than or equal to 2^15. If the group is not acceptable, the responder must reply with a Notify payload of type ATTRIBUTES-NOT-SUPPORTED, whose value is 13. Groups may also be negotiated directly in the security association proposal during Main Mode, either by passing all the component parts or by hiding them and passing only the group identifier in the clear.
sections.plainLanguage: The two peers have to agree which maths problem they both solve, and the memo lists four choices built in. If none of them is strong enough, the peers can agree a new one in a short second exchange and use it later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Confidentiality comes from the negotiated encryption algorithm and authentication from the negotiated method, which is a digital signature algorithm, a public key algorithm that supports encryption, or a pre-shared key. Both are only as good as the attributes negotiated as part of the ISAKMP security association.

Repeated re-keying with Quick Mode can consume the entropy of the Diffie-Hellman shared secret, so implementors should set a limit on the number of Quick Mode exchanges between exponentiations; the memo does not prescribe such a limit. Perfect forward secrecy of both key material and identities is possible, but it requires that only one non-ISAKMP security association be established per ISAKMP security association and that the ISAKMP security association then be deleted, so that a phase one negotiation is tied to a single phase two negotiation.

The strength of a key from a Diffie-Hellman exchange depends on the strength of the group, the size of the exponent and the entropy of the random number generator, so it is hard to determine. The default group, number one, used with a strong random number generator and an exponent of no less than 160 bits is sufficient to use for DES, and groups two through four give greater security. Nothing in IKE prevents the use of stronger groups, and elliptic curve groups will greatly increase strength using much smaller numbers; where the defined groups are not strong enough, New Group Mode can carry a group with the necessary strength, and it is up to implementations to check the primality of groups being offered and to reach their own strength estimates.

The memo also notes that the Diffie-Hellman exponents are assumed to be erased from memory after use and must not be derived from long-lived secrets such as the seed of a pseudo-random generator. Because IKE keeps a running initialization vector, an implementation should not update that vector until the decrypted message has passed a basic sanity check and has been shown to advance the state machine, so that retransmissions do not push the two sides out of step. Finally, while the last round trip of Main Mode and the last message of Aggressive Mode are encrypted, they are not strictly speaking authenticated, so an active substitution attack on the ciphertext could corrupt a payload, and corruption of an optional payload might not be detected at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The security of the whole scheme rests on the choices the two peers make in the first phase: a weak algorithm or a small secret cannot be fixed later. The memo also warns that the last message of the first phase is encrypted but not yet authenticated, so it is the weakest moment in the exchange.

items.title: SKEYID_d
items.text: Derived from SKEYID and the Diffie-Hellman shared secret. Used to derive keys for security associations other than ISAKMP.

items.title: SKEYID_a
items.text: Derived from SKEYID and SKEYID_d. Used to authenticate the messages of the ISAKMP security association.

items.title: SKEYID_e
items.text: Derived from SKEYID and SKEYID_a. Used to protect the confidentiality of the messages of the ISAKMP security association.
